name: Esther Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a normal workday look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on building sites fitting stairs, skirting and door frames, with some rough carpentry when a wall needs putting right. I have a vocational trade certificate and years of site work, but I am an ordinary experienced worker, not a supervisor. I enjoy making a stair feel solid underfoot; I hate finding a drawing that ignores the wall it is meant to fit. My partner Milan and I have two school-age children, a mortgage, and more than eight months of expenses saved. I earn well for this work and there are plenty of other contractors nearby. I have never used an AI tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the site team to use the quicker forms if they help, but keep the actual dimensions on the drawing. A stair has to fit the house, not a neat computer picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job and pay look safe in this mild version, and our savings give the family room. I do not want to be asked to sign a measured job from a form I cannot check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep fitting stairs and frames with the same measuring routine. In the first year I would mark any missing dimensions on the new order sheet before cutting timber.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. The children’s school day and the mortgage payment would look much as they do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which missing dimension matters most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rise and width of the top stair have to match the actual opening. I would measure twice before the tread is cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start using AI to make the form?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I have never used it and the mild change gives me no reason to add a tool between my tape and the job.

say: **Actual stair dimensions** belong on every building-site drawing before a carpenter cuts the timber.
**Quicker forms** do not replace site measurements.
think: My **high pay** and site work remain secure in the plateau.
Our **eight-month reserve** protects the family against a short interruption.
do: **Keep** fitting stairs and frames with the usual tape checks.
**Mark** missing dimensions before cutting timber from new order sheets.
S0.quote: A stair has to fit the house, not a neat computer picture.
fieldNote: She has **never used AI** and trusts the dimensions she measures personally at an old building site.
Her **high pay and savings** make the plateau financially secure.

steps.text: Keep fitting stairs and frames with usual site measurements

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the office can automate booking and buying, but it still needs to send the right material to site. The union safety meeting should hear from tradespeople before a shorter fitting target is adopted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect to keep my own hours for now because good stair fitting is in demand nearby. I worry the scheduler will squeeze the apprentices first, or send a standard kit where a crooked opening needs hand work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would record the measurements and fitting time on five non-standard stairs. During the first year I would take those examples to the site union meeting and ask for a target that includes checking and rework.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for younger workers, secure about my own wage. I know what a wrong kit can cost a day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which kit would expose a bad schedule?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A stair tread cut for a square opening will leave a gap against a bowed wall. I would show the measured gap next to the kit drawing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave this contractor if targets tighten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not on the first bad schedule. I have other contractors nearby, but I would try the union discussion and see what target the site actually adopts.

say: **Office booking and buying** change before capable robots can fit physical stairs on building sites.
**Tradespeople** should review shorter targets at the union meeting.
think: My **own hours** look secure because other nearby contractors still need experienced stair fitting and carpentry.
Apprentices may face **rushed kits** and squeezed time.
do: **Log** measurements and fitting time on five non-standard stairs.
**Bring** the examples to the site union meeting before targets change.
feel: **Uneasy** for younger workers, secure about personal pay.
S1.quote: A stair tread cut for a square opening will leave a gap against a bowed wall.
fieldNote: She names a **specific rework cost** rather than rejecting scheduling software in general.
Her **union action** is an actual site meeting, while a job move remains only a possibility.

steps.text: Bring five non-standard stair examples to site union meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that thinking AI by 2028 changes drawings, orders and booking, while capable building robots come around 2031. There are still about three years of hands-on stair and frame work in between.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot that can fit awkward stairs could cut my well-paid shifts after 2031. We have a cushion and plenty of contractors nearby, but the mortgage and two children mean I cannot assume a new post will pay as well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask our union group to observe a robot trial on a crooked stair and record who checks the final fit. In the first year after 2028 I would compare actual carpentry vacancies at two nearby contractors; if robots cut my hours after 2031, I would apply for a posted fitting job only if the wage covers our household bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but able to act before the pay changes. I can stand a trial of a building robot; I cannot let a child’s school bill depend on its brochure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the trial need to show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robot should measure the bowed wall itself, cut the tread, and leave a joint that does not rock. I would want the rejected pieces counted too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the nearby fitting job pays less?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Milan and I would compare the offer with the mortgage, school costs and our regular spending. We could accept less than my current wage, but not a monthly draw from savings.

say: **2028 thinking AI** reaches drawings before capable site robots around 2031.
**Stair fitting** remains physical during the gap.
think: Robots may cut my **well-paid shifts** after 2031.
Savings and **nearby contractors** help, but equal pay is uncertain.
do: **Observe** a crooked-stair robot trial with the union group.
**Apply** if robots cut hours after 2031 and wage covers household bills.
feel: **Anxious** about a pay cut, with options to investigate.
S2.quote: I can stand a trial of a building robot; I cannot let a child’s school bill depend on its brochure.
fieldNote: She uses a **union trial** to test fit quality and rejected material.
Her **job application** depends on actual reduced hours, a posted vacancy and bill-covering pay.

steps.text: Observe crooked-stair robot trial with union group
Apply for posted fitting job if robots cut hours and wage covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives a contractor time to show what a robot does on an old house before thinking AI arrives in 2031. Capable site robots follow about 2034, and I would want workers in the trial from the start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children will be older, but the mortgage may still be there. I might take a quality-checking role if it involves real site work; I will not leave a good wage for a course with no job at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the contractor for a hands-on trial and a written pay scale for site quality work. If a real local quality-checking vacancy offers employer-paid training and a wage that covers our bills, I would take the training before 2031 and apply after 2031; otherwise I would keep fitting stairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wary, though the longer runway lets me judge an actual offer. A machine working on a clean demonstration floor does not tell me how it fits an old stair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you inspect in a quality job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check tread height, joints, handrail fixing and whether the steps feel solid. A photograph alone would not satisfy me when checking a robot-fitted stair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Milan support the move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Milan would want the wage and hours written down before we decide together. I expect support if the job covers our bills and keeps time for the children.

say: **Old-house trials** should come before capable site robots around 2034.
**Worker input** belongs in the trial from the start.
think: A **quality role** could suit me if it includes real site checks.
I will not trade **good wages** for a course without a vacancy.
do: **Request** a hands-on trial and written quality-role pay scale.
**Take** employer-paid training only for a real local bill-covering vacancy.
**Apply** for quality work after 2031 if trained; otherwise keep fitting stairs.
feel: **Wary**, but able to judge a documented offer.
S3.quote: A photograph alone would not satisfy me when checking a robot-fitted stair.
fieldNote: Her **training condition** combines employer payment, local vacancy and wages.
Her **quality checks** remain physical, matching her reluctance to trust screen output alone on an old stair.

steps.text: Keep fitting stairs while requesting a hands-on robot trial
Take employer-paid quality training for real local bill-covering vacancy
Apply after 2031 if trained and posted local site quality job covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade puts thinking AI in 2036 and capable building robots around 2039. The children will be older by then, and I would still expect to work unless we have deliberately chosen a different path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be in my fifties when field robots arrive, with a mortgage balance I cannot predict today. Our savings give us time, but a robot could still take the better-paid fitting jobs I had counted on in later years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep doing carpentry now and review the mortgage with Milan each year. In the first year after 2036 I would apply for local site quality work only if a genuine opening pays enough to cover our bills; I would ask our union site group to press for workers to be able to reject unsafe robot-fitted stairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with plenty of time to plan. I do not want a machine deciding whether a stair is safe just because the house owner cannot see the joint.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should a worker be able to reject?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A loose handrail or uneven tread after a robot fitting should be sent back before anyone uses the stair. The worker who measures a robot-fitted stair needs authority to say no before anyone uses it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you save differently now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the money we have put by is our cushion, and we would not spend it on an unproven machine. We will review the mortgage as the children get older.

say: **2036 thinking AI** precedes capable building robots that can fit physical stairs around 2039.
**Worker rejection** should cover unsafe robot-fitted stairs.
think: Better-paid **stair work** could shrink in later years.
Our **savings** give time, though the mortgage balance remains unknown.
do: **Keep** carpentry work and review the mortgage annually.
**Apply** for local quality work after 2036 only with real bill-covering pay.
**Ask** the union site group to protect worker rejection of unsafe stairs.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to protect later earnings.
S4.quote: The worker who measures a robot-fitted stair needs authority to say no before anyone uses it.
fieldNote: She keeps **existing reserves** separate from new saving; no save-more action is recorded.
Her **union request** concerns a concrete unsafe handrail or uneven tread, not a general slogan.

steps.text: Keep carpentry work and review mortgage with Milan annually
Apply for local site quality work after 2036 only with real bill-covering pay
Ask union site group to protect worker rejection of unsafe stairs

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because capable robots around 2031 might cut my well-paid stair-fitting shifts while we still have a mortgage and school bills. A paid route into a real local quality job and authority to reject unsafe work would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who signs off a stair after a robot fits it. I want a carpenter standing on the tread before anybody is asked to trust the photograph.

portrait: **Esther Petrov**, 43, is an experienced construction worker with a vocational trade certificate who fits stairs and frames.
She and partner Milan have **two school-age children**, a mortgage, high trade pay and over eight months saved.
She has **never used AI** and trusts physical measurements and joints over site drawings or machine photos.
In **Steady Disruption**, she takes five non-standard stair examples to a union site meeting while expecting her pay to hold.
The **2028 picture** worries her because a robot might cut well-paid shifts; longer lead time makes quality work possible.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut high-paid stair-fitting shifts after 2031 while mortgage and school costs continue.
whatWouldHelp: Employer-paid **quality training** linked to a real local job at bill-covering pay would give her another option.
Worker **rejection authority** would keep unsafe robot-fitted stairs from being accepted.
headlineQuote: I want a carpenter standing on the tread before anybody is asked to trust the photograph.
